newsitem.title: GREECE: Moody's upgrading draws Greece closer to EMU.
newsitem.headline: Moody's upgrading draws Greece closer to EMU.

text.p: Bankers and economists hailed Moody's upgrading of Greece's sovereign ceiling on foreign loans, saying it would lower its debt servicing and help it attain its goal of being in the second wave of EMU countries.
Moody's Investors Service said on Monday it had upgraded the sovereign ceilings for long-term foreign-currency bonds and bank deposits of Greece to Baa1 from Baa3.
Moody's also raised the sovereign ceiling for short-term notes and deposits to Prime-2 from Prime-3.
It cited improvement in the fiscal balances in the past few years as well as the stronger political resolve to continue with policies consistent with EU convergence.
"On the macroeconomic front, the economy has begun expanding thanks to the robust growth of investment, both private and public," Moody's said in a statement.

Industrial production has picked up and manufacturing employment has stopped falling. Inflation has been reduced to single digits for the first time in two decades and confidence has been established in the drachma, it said.

"It is a very positive and welcome development. It gives Greece the opportunity to negotiate lower interest rates on the foreign component of its public debt," George Spelios, treasurer at private ErgoBank, said.

Asked if smaller spreads over benchmarks paid by Greece on its foreign currency loans in the last year already reflected a better credit standing, he said the lower spreads discounted partly the improved creditworthiness of the country.

"Many foreign institutonal investors are conservative and act only after major credit agencies such as Moody's raise sovereign ceilings, so Greece can achieve much better terms on its foreign borrowing following the upgrading," he said.
Greece paid spreads of 100 basis points plus over benchmarks on its foreign currency loans a year or so ago, but margins have narrowed to around 60 basis points or less, dealers said.
Greece's domestic debt is not rated by international credit agencies, partly due to the lack of regular, frequent releases of data on public domestic debt.
"Moody's announcement is good news for the economy. It is the natural reward for an economic policy that is consistent with Maastricht," said Nikos Sikiaridis, treasurer at Barclays Bank PLc, Athens.

"It is a positive development which reflects the gradual improvement in economic fundamentals in the last few years," said Michalis Masourakis, head of the economics research department at private Alpha Credit Bank.
Masourakis added that international markets had partly discounted the credit upgrading which would help Greece in its effort to be in the second wave of countries joining the EMU.

"The markets have already factored in part of the upgrading in the last year or so but it is still good news for Greece that could see its foreign currency borrowing costs drop further and help close the budget gap," he said.
"It definitely provides a boost to Greece's efforts to be in the EMU sooner rather than later," said Masourakis.
Prime Minister Costas Simitis has said that he would like Greece to join economic and monetary union (EMU) by 2001.
Other market players said the upgrading would improve Greece's image in general.

"The upgrading improves Greece's image in the international markets, boosts the credibility of its economic policy and draws it closer to its EMU target via lower interest payments on its budget," said Spyros Kordopatis, treasurer at Credit Lyonnais.

Greece is the only EU country that does not meet a single Maastricht criteria despite progress in its fiscal front, inflation, interest rates in the 1990s. --Dimitris Kontogiannis, Athens Newsroom +301 3311812-4
